about: Molecule lab settings and words. 'ui' holds every visitor-facing word by key: placeholders until COPYWRITER MAIN writes them. Keep the {braces}. No em dashes. Facts live in 'elements' and 'challenges' and point at sources.json keys. Named compounds and formulas come from compounds.json (built from PubChem by tools/lab_build.py). Check with python tools/lab_check.py.
elementsNote: valences = usual numbers of covalent bonds (H 1 and the octet rule: C 4, N 3, O 2, Cl 1; P 3 or 5 and S 2, 4 or 6 as in PCl5 and SF6, os-chem-7-3). ve = valence electrons from the Lewis symbol (os-chem-7-3), used only for lone pairs. charges = cation charges (group 1 1+, group 2 2+, iron 2+ or 3+, os-chem-2-6). anion = gains electrons in an ionic bond (group 16 2-, group 17 1-, os-chem-2-6). Fe radius is the low-spin value. radius in pm (cordero-2008), colour from jmol-colors.

ui.model.note: Simplified model. Shapes follow the VSEPR idea that bonds and lone pairs spread out; lengths and angles are drawn, not measured.
ui.tab.label: Lab panels
ui.atom.empty: Tap an atom on the bench (or choose Details in list mode) to see its bonds, its shape and its orbitals.
ui.atom.orbitalsNote: The atom on its own, before bonding: its electrons in orbitals.
ui.shapeAbout.linear: Two regions sit on opposite sides: 180 degrees.
ui.shapeAbout.trigonalPlanar: Three regions spread flat: 120 degrees apart.
ui.shapeAbout.tetrahedral: Four regions point to the corners of a tetrahedron: 109.5 degrees apart.
ui.shapeAbout.trigonalPyramidal: Four regions, one a lone pair. The lone pair takes more room, so the bond angles close a little below 109.5 degrees.
ui.shapeAbout.bent: The lone pairs take more room than bonds and squeeze the bonds together. In water the angle is 104.5 degrees.
ui.shapeAbout.trigonalBipyramidal: Five regions: three around the middle at 120 degrees, two at the top and bottom at 90 degrees to them.
ui.shapeAbout.octahedral: Six regions point to the corners of an octahedron.

ui.why.self: An atom cannot bond to itself.
ui.why.gone: That atom is no longer on the bench.
ui.why.metalMetal: {a} and {b} are both metals. In this lab metals bond by handing electrons to a nonmetal, so two metals do not bond here.
ui.why.metalPartner: {metal} is a metal. Here it hands electrons to oxygen, sulfur or chlorine, which can take them. {el} is not one of those in this lab.
ui.why.metalFull: {metal} has already handed over {used} electrons, and it gives up to {charge}.
ui.why.anionFull: {el} has room for {max} more electrons from bonds, and it already has {used}.
ui.why.expandedNoIon: {el} is using an expanded octet, so in this lab it cannot also take electrons from a metal.
ui.why.hydrogen: Hydrogen needs only two electrons, so it makes just one single bond.
ui.why.full: {el} already makes {used} bonds and usually makes at most {max}. Each bond shares one pair of electrons, and the octet is full.
ui.why.fullOrder: A {order}-bond here would give {el} more than {max} bonds.
ui.why.fullIon: {el} took electrons from a metal, so it stays at its basic bond count of {max}.
ui.why.maxTriple: Three shared pairs (a triple bond) is the most two atoms share here.
ui.why.ionMax: That ionic link already carries as many electrons as these atoms can hand over.
ui.live.ionic: {a} and {b}: ionic bond, {n} electrons handed over.
ui.live.gave: Atoms for {formula} are on the bench. Now bond them.
ui.sources.title: Sources
ui.sources.pubchem: Every named compound and challenge target was checked against PubChem ({n} records):
ui.challenge.water.title: Water
ui.challenge.water.goal: Join two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom.
ui.challenge.water.hint: Oxygen makes two bonds and hydrogen makes one.
ui.challenge.water.win: Two lone pairs on the oxygen push the hydrogens together, so water is bent at 104.5 degrees. Turn on Lone pairs to see them.
ui.challenge.methane.title: Methane
ui.challenge.methane.goal: Give one carbon atom four hydrogen partners.
ui.challenge.methane.hint: Select the carbon, then tap H four times.
ui.challenge.methane.win: Four bonds and no lone pairs: a tetrahedron, 109.5 degrees between bonds. Methane is the main part of natural gas.
ui.challenge.ammonia.title: Ammonia
ui.challenge.ammonia.goal: Bond hydrogen atoms to one nitrogen atom until it is complete.
ui.challenge.ammonia.hint: Nitrogen makes three bonds and keeps one lone pair.
ui.challenge.ammonia.win: Three bonds and one lone pair make a trigonal pyramid. The lone pair squeezes the H-N-H angles a little below 109.5 degrees.
ui.challenge.oxygen.title: Oxygen gas
ui.challenge.oxygen.goal: Join two oxygen atoms so each one is complete.
ui.challenge.oxygen.hint: Each oxygen makes two bonds. One single bond leaves each needing one more. Drop one oxygen on the other again.
ui.challenge.oxygen.win: Each oxygen makes two bonds, so the pair shares a double bond.
ui.challenge.carbon-dioxide.title: Carbon dioxide
ui.challenge.carbon-dioxide.goal: One carbon, two oxygens, every atom complete.
ui.challenge.carbon-dioxide.hint: Carbon makes four bonds and each oxygen makes two. Try double bonds.
ui.challenge.carbon-dioxide.win: Each double bond counts as one region, and two regions sit opposite each other: carbon dioxide is a straight line.
ui.challenge.ethanol.title: Ethanol
ui.challenge.ethanol.goal: Two carbons, one oxygen and six hydrogens, with an O-H group on the end.
ui.challenge.ethanol.hint: Chain them C-C-O, then use Fill with H.
ui.challenge.ethanol.win: The same atoms joined C-O-C make dimethyl ether instead. Same formula, different molecule: those are isomers.
ui.challenge.glycine.title: Glycine
ui.challenge.glycine.goal: Build the amino acid glycine: an amino group (N), a carbon, and a carboxyl group (C and two O).
ui.challenge.glycine.hint: Chain N-C-C. Give the end carbon one double-bonded O and one single-bonded O, then Fill with H.
ui.challenge.glycine.win: Glycine's side chain (its R group) is a single hydrogen atom.
ui.challenge.glucose.title: Glucose
ui.challenge.glucose.goal: The big one: six carbons, twelve hydrogens, six oxygens. A chain or a ring both count.
ui.challenge.glucose.hint: Make a chain of six carbons. Put a double-bonded O on the first carbon and an O on each of the others, then Fill with H.
ui.challenge.glucose.win: Glucose is the sugar cells break down to make ATP. In water most glucose closes into a ring.
ui.challenge.glucose.forms: Both the open chain and the ring count. The lab checks which atoms connect, not their left or right handedness, so sugars that differ only in handedness match too.
ui.challenge.sodium-chloride.title: Table salt (bonus)
ui.challenge.sodium-chloride.goal: Drop a sodium atom on a chlorine atom.
ui.challenge.sodium-chloride.hint: A metal and a nonmetal make an ionic bond.
ui.challenge.sodium-chloride.win: Sodium hands one electron to chlorine: Na+ and Cl- hold together by an ionic bond. Real salt is a crystal of many ions, not single molecules.
ui.challenge.hydrogen-cyanide.title: Hydrogen cyanide (bonus)
ui.challenge.hydrogen-cyanide.goal: One hydrogen, one carbon, one nitrogen, all complete.
ui.challenge.hydrogen-cyanide.hint: Carbon and nitrogen need a triple bond.
ui.challenge.hydrogen-cyanide.win: Carbon and nitrogen share three pairs of electrons: a triple bond.
